o: We need the length of the longest string that is a subsequence of exactly one string in `strs` and not a subsequence of any other. The crucial observation is that if any uncommon subsequence exists, an optimal one is always one of the input strings itself: extending a subsequence to its full parent string can only make it 'less common' (harder to be a subsequence of others). So we only need to test whether each string is a subsequence of some *other* string. In Example 1, "eae" is not a subsequence of "aba" or "cdc", so the answer is 3. In Example 2, every string is a subsequence of another ("aa" ⊂ "aaa"), so nothing qualifies and we return -1. With n ≤ 50 and lengths ≤ 10, even checking all pairs is trivially fast.
k: If an uncommon subsequence exists, some full input string is itself an uncommon subsequence — never look at proper subsequences.
A string s is disqualified exactly when it is a subsequence of another string t with |t| ≥ |s|.
The classic two-pointer greedy correctly tests 'is s a subsequence of t' in linear time.

a.i: For every string, scan all other strings and test whether it is a subsequence of them. If it is a subsequence of none, it is uncommon; track the maximum length. This directly implements the key insight without any preprocessing.
s: Define isSub(s, t): greedily match characters of s inside t using two pointers.
For each string strs[i], assume it is uncommon.
For every j ≠ i, if isSub(strs[i], strs[j]), mark strs[i] as common and stop.
If strs[i] survived, update the answer with len(strs[i]).
Return the maximum found, or -1 if none survived.
a.t: O(n^2 · L) where n ≤ 50 is the number of strings and L ≤ 10 the max length — each pair needs one linear subsequence check.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the input.

a.n: Approach 2: Sort by Length Descending + Early Exit
a.i: Sort strings by decreasing length. A string can only be a subsequence of strings at least as long as itself, so when scanning in this order we only compare each candidate against previously seen (longer or equal-length) strings. The first string that is not a subsequence of any earlier string is the answer, since it has maximal length among survivors. Equal duplicates are handled naturally because a duplicate appears later and matches an earlier copy.
s: Sort strs by length descending (ties broken arbitrarily).
Iterate strings in order; for each candidate at index i, check it against strs[0..i-1] only.
Use the two-pointer test to see if the candidate is a subsequence of any earlier string.
If it is a subsequence of none, return its length immediately.
a.t: O(n log n · L + n^2 · L) — sorting plus pairwise checks restricted to earlier (longer-or-equal) strings; asymptotically same as brute force but often faster in practice due to early exit.
a.sp: O(1) or O(n) depending on the language's sort implementation.

w: In an interview, lead with the key insight (the answer is always some full string), then present Approach 2 as the clean solution; Approach 1 is fine to mention as the direct brute force. Common pitfalls: forgetting that equal strings disqualify each other (duplicates must fail), testing only strictly longer strings incorrectly when ties exist (comparing against all earlier strings after sorting handles ties safely), and trying to enumerate actual subsequences, which is unnecessary and exponential. Edge cases: all strings identical → -1; a unique longest string → its length immediately. Follow-ups might ask for the count of uncommon subsequences or handling much larger inputs, where grouping by length and pruning by character sets would matter.
